title: The Clever Octopus
summary: How the octopus uses its soft, boneless body, sucker-covered arms, color-changing skin, ink and unusual brain to survive in the sea, and why scientists call it clever.
poll: An octopus is smarter than most people think.

versions.title: The Smart Octopus
versions.text:
This is an octopus. It lives in the sea. It has eight arms. Some live in the Red Sea.

It has no bones. Its body is soft. The one hard part is its beak. So it can squeeze through a tiny hole.

Each arm has lots of suckers. The suckers grab things. They can taste, too!

It can hide well. It can change its skin fast. It can look like a rock. Then big fish do not see it. But what if a fish sees it? It squirts ink. The ink makes a dark cloud. Then it swims off.

It is smart. It has a big brain. But most of its nerve cells are in its arms. It can solve a puzzle. It can open a jar to get food. Some take shells to use as a home.

It has three hearts. Its blood is blue!

Most live just one or two years. A mom guards her eggs. She does not eat. She dies when they hatch.

Each of its eight arms is covered with round suckers. The suckers can grab and hold things tight. They can also taste and feel what they touch.

An octopus is very good at hiding. In less than a second, it can change the color of its skin. It can make its skin bumpy, so it looks like a rock. A hungry fish may still find it. Then the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink. It swims away fast.

Octopuses are clever. An octopus has a large brain. But most of its nerve cells are in its arms. Octopuses can solve a puzzle. Some can open a jar to get the food inside. Some even carry coconut shells to hide in.

An octopus has three hearts. Its blood is blue.

Most octopuses live for just one or two years. A mother guards her eggs. She does not eat. She dies soon after the babies hatch.

versions.text:

An octopus has no bones at all. The only hard part of its body is a sharp beak. It uses the beak to crack open crabs. The rest of its body is soft. So an octopus can squeeze through any gap that is bigger than its beak.

Each arm has rows of round suckers. The suckers grip things tightly. But they do more than that. They can also taste and feel whatever they touch.

An octopus is an expert at hiding. Special cells in its skin let it change color in less than a second. It can also raise small bumps, so its skin looks like a rock or seaweed. A hungry fish may find it anyway. Then the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink and darts away.

Octopuses are very clever. An octopus has a large brain, yet most of its nerve cells are in its arms. In aquariums, octopuses have solved a puzzle box. They have opened a jar to reach food inside. Some even carry coconut shells to use as a shelter.

An octopus also has three hearts. Its blood is blue instead of red.

Sadly, most octopuses live for only one or two years. A mother guards her eggs for weeks without eating. She dies soon after the babies hatch.

On the sandy sea floor, a soft animal with eight arms slides between the rocks. It is an octopus, one of the most surprising animals in the ocean. Octopuses live in seas all around the world. Some live in the warm Red Sea, along Saudi Arabia's west coast.

An octopus is a mollusk. That means it is related to snails and clams. But unlike them, it has no shell and no bones. The only hard part of its body is a sharp beak. It uses the beak to crack open crabs. The rest of its body is soft, so an octopus can squeeze through any gap that is larger than its beak.

Each arm is lined with rows of suckers. The suckers grip rocks and food tightly. They can also taste and feel whatever they touch.

An octopus is a master of camouflage. Special cells in its skin let it change color in less than a second. It can also change the texture of its skin. It raises little bumps so it looks like a rock or a patch of seaweed. If a predator such as a shark spots it anyway, the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink and shoots away.

Scientists agree that octopuses are intelligent. An octopus has a large brain, but most of its nerve cells are in its arms. In aquariums, octopuses have solved puzzles and opened jars to reach food. Some wild octopuses even carry coconut shells to use as a shelter.

An octopus also has three hearts. Its blood is blue instead of red.

Most octopuses live for only one or two years. A mother guards her eggs for weeks without eating. She dies soon after the babies hatch.

versions.text:
On the sandy floor of the sea, a soft-bodied animal with eight flexible arms glides silently between the rocks, searching for its next meal. It is an octopus, one of the most remarkable creatures in the ocean. Octopuses live in seas throughout the world, including the warm waters of the Red Sea along Saudi Arabia's western coast.

An octopus belongs to a group of animals called mollusks, which also includes snails, clams, and oysters. Unlike most of its relatives, however, an octopus has no protective shell and no bones at all. The only hard part of its body is a sharp, parrot-like beak, which it uses to crack open crabs and shellfish. Because the rest of its body is completely soft, an octopus can squeeze through any opening that is larger than its beak.

Each of its eight arms is lined with rows of powerful suckers. These suckers grip rocks and prey firmly, and they can also taste and feel whatever they touch.

The octopus is an expert at camouflage. Special cells in its skin allow it to change color in less than a second, and it can also alter the texture of its skin, raising tiny bumps so that it resembles a rock or a clump of seaweed. If a predator such as a shark or an eel discovers it anyway, the octopus releases a cloud of dark ink and jets away while the attacker is confused.

Scientists consider octopuses to be highly intelligent animals. An octopus has a large brain, yet most of its nerve cells are actually located in its arms. In aquariums, octopuses have solved complicated puzzles and unscrewed jars to reach food. Some wild octopuses even collect coconut shells and carry them across the sea floor to use as a portable shelter.

Remarkably, an octopus also has three hearts, and its blood is blue rather than red.

versions.title: The Clever Octopus
versions.text:
On the sandy floor of the sea, a soft-bodied animal with eight flexible arms glides silently between the rocks, investigating every crevice in search of its next meal. It is an octopus, one of the most remarkable creatures in the ocean. Octopuses inhabit seas throughout the world, including the warm waters of the Red Sea along Saudi Arabia's western coast.

An octopus belongs to a group of animals called mollusks, which also includes snails, clams, and oysters, and like every mollusk it is an invertebrate, meaning an animal without a backbone. Unlike most of its relatives, however, an octopus possesses no protective shell and no bones whatsoever. The only hard structure in its body is a sharp, parrot-like beak, which it uses to crack open crabs and other shellfish. Because the remainder of its body is entirely soft, an octopus can squeeze through any opening that is larger than its beak.

Each of its eight arms is lined with rows of powerful suckers. These suckers grip rocks and prey firmly. They can also taste and feel whatever they touch.

The octopus is a champion of camouflage. Its skin contains thousands of tiny sacs filled with pigment, and by stretching or squeezing these sacs, it can change color in less than a second, and it can also alter the texture of its skin, raising tiny bumps so that it closely resembles a rock or a clump of seaweed. If a predator such as a shark or an eel discovers it anyway, the octopus releases a cloud of dark ink. Then it jets away while the attacker is confused.

Scientists consider octopuses to be exceptionally intelligent invertebrates. An octopus has roughly 500 million nerve cells, or neurons, yet about two-thirds of them are located in its arms rather than its brain. Researchers who study octopus cognition have watched captive animals solve complicated puzzles and unscrew jars to retrieve food. Certain wild octopuses even collect coconut shells and carry them across the sea floor to use as a portable shelter.

Remarkably, an octopus also has three hearts, and its blood is blue rather than red because it uses a substance containing copper to carry oxygen.

Despite their impressive intelligence, most octopuses live for only one or two years. A mother will brood her eggs for several weeks without eating, and she dies shortly after her babies hatch.

The octopus is a mollusk, a member of the same broad group as snails, clams, and oysters, and like all mollusks it is an invertebrate, meaning an animal without a backbone. Unlike most of its relatives, however, it possesses no protective shell and no bones whatsoever. The only rigid structure in its body is a sharp, parrot-like beak, which it uses to crack open crabs and shellfish, and because the remainder of its body is entirely soft, an octopus can squeeze through any opening larger than that beak.

It can also alter the texture of its skin, raising small bumps so that it resembles a rock or a clump of seaweed. Scientists regard octopuses as some of the most intelligent invertebrates on Earth. An octopus has roughly 500 million nerve cells, or neurons, yet about two-thirds of them are located in its arms rather than its brain. Researchers studying octopus cognition have repeatedly observed captive animals solve puzzles and unscrew jars to retrieve food, and certain wild octopuses even carry coconut shells across the sea floor to use as a portable shelter.

Remarkably, an octopus also has three hearts, and its blood is blue rather than red because it relies on a copper-based substance to carry oxygen.

Despite this impressive intelligence, most octopuses live for only one or two years. A mother will brood her eggs for weeks without eating, and she dies shortly after her babies hatch.

versions.title: The Clever Octopus
versions.text:
On the sandy floor of the sea, a soft-bodied animal with eight flexible arms glides silently between the rocks, methodically investigating every crevice in search of its next meal. It is an octopus, one of the most extraordinary creatures in the ocean, and it inhabits seas throughout the world, including the warm waters of the Red Sea along Saudi Arabia's western coast.

The octopus is a mollusk, a member of the same diverse group as snails, clams, and oysters, and like every mollusk it is an invertebrate, an animal without a backbone. Unlike most of its relatives, however, it possesses neither a protective shell nor any bones. The only rigid structure in its body is a sharp, parrot-like beak, which it uses to crack open crabs and shellfish, and because the remainder of its body is entirely flexible, an octopus can squeeze through any opening larger than that beak.

Each of its eight arms is lined with rows of muscular suckers, which grip rocks and prey securely and can also taste and feel whatever they contact.

The octopus is an extraordinary master of camouflage. Its skin contains thousands of specialized sacs filled with pigment, and by expanding or contracting these sacs with tiny muscles, the animal can transform its color in less than a second. It can simultaneously modify the texture of its skin, raising small bumps so that it convincingly resembles a rock or a clump of seaweed. If a predator such as a shark or an eel detects it anyway, the octopus releases a cloud of dark ink and jets away while its attacker is temporarily confused.

Scientists regard octopuses as among the most intelligent invertebrates on Earth. An octopus possesses roughly 500 million nerve cells, or neurons, yet approximately two-thirds of them are located in its arms rather than its central brain, which allows each arm considerable independence. Researchers investigating octopus cognition have observed captive animals solving puzzles and unscrewing jars to retrieve food, and certain wild octopuses even transport coconut shells across the sea floor to use as a portable shelter.

Remarkably, an octopus also has three hearts, and its blood is blue rather than red because it relies on a copper-based substance to carry oxygen.

Despite this impressive intelligence, most octopuses live for only one or two years. A mother will brood her eggs for several weeks without eating, and she dies shortly after her offspring hatch.

versions.title: The Clever Octopus
versions.text:
Gliding silently between the rocks on the sandy floor of the sea, a soft-bodied animal with eight flexible arms methodically investigates every crevice in search of its next meal. This is the octopus, one of the most extraordinary organisms in the ocean, and it inhabits seas throughout the world, including the warm, coral-rich waters of the Red Sea along Saudi Arabia's western coast.

Biologically, the octopus is a mollusk, belonging to the same diverse group as snails, clams, and oysters, and like every mollusk it is an invertebrate, an animal that lacks a backbone. Unlike most of its relatives, however, it possesses neither a protective shell nor any internal skeleton. The only rigid structure in its body is a sharp, parrot-like beak, which it employs to crack open crabs and shellfish, and because the remainder of its anatomy is entirely flexible, an octopus can squeeze through any opening marginally larger than that beak.

Each of its eight arms is lined with rows of muscular suckers, which grip surfaces and prey securely while simultaneously tasting and feeling whatever they contact.

The octopus is an exceptional practitioner of camouflage. Its skin contains thousands of specialized elastic sacs filled with pigment, and by expanding or contracting these sacs with microscopic muscles, the animal can transform its coloration in less than a second. It can simultaneously modify the texture of its skin, raising small projections so that it convincingly imitates a rock or a clump of seaweed. Should a predator such as a shark or an eel detect it nevertheless, the octopus discharges a cloud of dark ink and propels itself away while its attacker is temporarily disoriented.

Scientists consider octopuses to be among the most intelligent invertebrates on the planet. An octopus possesses approximately 500 million nerve cells, or neurons, yet roughly two-thirds of them are distributed throughout its arms rather than concentrated in its central brain, which grants each arm considerable independence. Researchers investigating octopus cognition have documented captive individuals solving puzzles and unscrewing jars to retrieve food, and certain wild octopuses even transport coconut shells across the sea floor to use as a portable shelter.

Remarkably, an octopus also has three hearts, and its blood is blue rather than red because it depends on a copper-based molecule to transport oxygen.

Despite this considerable intelligence, most octopuses survive for only one or two years. A mother will brood her eggs for several weeks without feeding, and she perishes shortly after her offspring hatch.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How octopuses swim faster than all the fish in the sea
How an octopus's body and brain help it survive
Why the Red Sea is warm
questions.why: Most of the article tells about the octopus's soft body, arms, hiding tricks and smart brain.

wrong.A: The article never says octopuses are faster than fish.
wrong.C: The Red Sea is named only as a place octopuses live.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about catching octopuses.

questions.stem: What is the only hard part of an octopus's body?
questions.why: The article says the one hard part of its body is its beak.

wrong.A: The arms are soft and bend easily.
wrong.B: The suckers grab and taste; they are not hard.
wrong.D: The skin is soft and can change color.

questions.stem: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.why: The article says an octopus has three hearts.

wrong.A: People have one heart, but an octopus has more.
wrong.B: Two is not the number in the article.
wrong.C: Eight is the number of arms, not hearts.

questions.stem: Why can an octopus squeeze through a tiny hole?
questions.why: The article says it has no bones and a soft body, so it can squeeze through small spaces.

wrong.B: Long arms do not help it fit through a small hole.
wrong.C: Ink helps it get away, not fit into holes.
wrong.D: Its hearts have nothing to do with fitting through holes.

questions.stem: Changing color most likely helps an octopus —
options: swim faster than a big fish
questions.why: When it looks like a rock, hungry fish do not see it, so it stays safe.

wrong.A: Color does not change how fast it swims.
wrong.B: The article does not link color to eggs.
wrong.D: The suckers taste food, not the skin color.

questions.stem: Which fact best shows that an octopus is smart?
options: It has blood that is blue, not red.
It can open a jar to get food.
questions.why: Opening a jar means it has to figure out a problem, which shows it is smart.

wrong.A: Blue blood is a body fact, not a sign of being smart.
wrong.C: Many animals live in the sea; that does not show it is smart.
wrong.D: Having eight arms does not show thinking.

questions.stem: The article says an octopus can squeeze through a small hole. What does squeeze mean?
options: Bite something very hard with a beak
questions.why: To squeeze through a hole is to push your body through a space that is very tight.

wrong.A: Biting is done with the beak, not squeezing.
wrong.B: Changing color is a different skill.
wrong.C: Swimming fast does not mean going through a small space.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about the octopus's ink?

To show how the eggs hatch
questions.why: The ink makes a dark cloud so the octopus can escape a big fish.

wrong.B: Octopuses do not write; the ink is for escaping.
wrong.D: The ink has nothing to do with eggs.

If a predator still finds it, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and shoot away.

MID.prompt: Explain how an octopus uses camouflage and ink together to stay safe from predators. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained how camouflage helps the octopus.
I explained when and why it uses ink.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: An octopus's camouflage lets special cells in its skin change color in less than a second and even raise bumps to copy the texture of a rock or seaweed, so a predator swimming past may never notice it is there at all. If camouflage fails and a predator such as a shark spots it anyway, the intelligent octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink to confuse the attacker and then shoots away while the predator is distracted. Using camouflage first and ink only as a last resort shows how this clever mollusk layers its defenses to stay safe.

wrong.C: This number is far too large.
wrong.D: Eight is the number of arms, not a count of neurons.

questions.stem: What in the octopus's skin allows it to change color?
questions.why: The article explains that the skin contains thousands of sacs of pigment that the octopus stretches or squeezes.

wrong.C: Ink is released as a cloud for escape, not used to change skin color.
wrong.D: Copper is linked to its blue blood, not its skin color.

questions.stem: The article says a mother octopus will brood her eggs without eating. What does brood mean?
options: To leave behind and swim away from
questions.why: The mother stays with her eggs for weeks to protect them until they hatch.

wrong.A: The sentence says she does not eat.
wrong.B: She stays with the eggs instead of leaving them.
wrong.C: Ink is used for escape, not for caring for eggs.

questions.stem: About two-thirds of an octopus's neurons are in its arms. What can a reader infer from this?
options: The octopus's brain does no real work at all in its body.
Each arm can sense and react partly on its own.
Its arms grow back very quickly.
questions.why: The article says this arrangement gives each arm considerable independence, so the arms can respond partly by themselves.

wrong.A: The octopus still has a central brain; the article does not say it is useless.
wrong.C: The article says nothing about arms growing back.
wrong.D: The article describes octopuses solving puzzles, which shows they learn.

questions.stem: What does the mother octopus's behavior suggest?
options: She cannot recognize her own eggs.
She swims away and leaves the eggs as soon as they are laid.
She puts protecting her eggs ahead of her own survival.
She is hunting for coconut shells.
questions.why: She stops eating to guard her eggs and dies soon after they hatch, which suggests the eggs come first.

wrong.A: She guards them for weeks, which shows she knows they are hers.
wrong.B: The article says she stays with them for weeks.
wrong.D: Coconut shells are used as shelters, not linked to the mother here.

questions.stem: Why is an octopus's blood blue?
options: It relies on a copper-based substance to carry oxygen.
It drinks large amounts of salty seawater every single day.
Its three hearts pump very quickly.
questions.why: The article explains that a copper-based substance carries oxygen in its blood, which makes the blood blue.

wrong.B: The article does not connect seawater to its blood color.
wrong.C: Its diet is not given as the reason.
wrong.D: The article mentions three hearts but does not say they cause the blue color.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention snails, clams and oysters?
options: To list the foods an octopus prefers
To compare how fast different sea animals move
To describe the animals of the Red Sea
To show which group of animals the octopus belongs to
questions.why: The author names them to explain that the octopus is a mollusk, like these animals.

wrong.A: The octopus is described eating crabs and shellfish; snails are named as relatives.
wrong.C: They are named as relatives, not as a description of the Red Sea.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say the octopus is the most impressive animal in the sea. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that the octopus is the most impressive invertebrate in the sea. The article notes that although most of its neurons are packed into its arms rather than its brain, octopuses have still solved puzzles and unscrewed jars in aquariums, which demonstrates a genuine cognition unusual for a creature without a backbone. Its body is equally remarkable, since it can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak and instantly change both the color and the texture of its skin, abilities that together show a combination of intelligence and physical adaptation that few other sea animals can match.
